svg.aria-label: Azure deployment pipeline end to end: the run signs in through a per-tenant federated credential with no stored secret; nothing exists in the subscription beforehand, so every application secret travels with the run and Terraform must apply twice, once to create the registry and again once the images are pushed.

g.text: Azure — one tenant, from form submission to a running chatbot
The subscription is empty until the run starts, which forces both of this pipeline's distinguishing features: secrets in the run, and two applies.
WHAT THE PLATFORM AND THE RUN DO, IN ORDER
WHAT EXISTS IN THE CUSTOMER'S AZURE SUBSCRIPTION
At onboarding, before any run exists
The platform generates the signer secret and encrypts it, along with the LLM key,
and the Pinecone key. It holds no Azure credential; the customer trusts the run instead.
No Azure call is possible here — there is no vault to write to, and no ARN to keep.
Only what the customer's setup created
The resource group, the deployment identity and the state storage.
The identity's federated credential trusts this tenant's runs. There is no vault yet,
so the run fetches every app secret it needs from the platform, once, by OIDC token.
Notify the platform, then fetch this tenant's secrets by OIDC
Unpack the config bundle
Compute the deterministic resource names
Pull both golden images from the platform's own registry
Sign in to the subscription through federation — no secret
terraform init, against state in the customer's own storage, locked
terraform apply, first pass — targeted
Sign in to the new registry, retag and push both images
terraform apply, second pass — the full graph
Read the outputs, then push the signer's function code
Upload the outputs as a run artifact and notify the platform
released once, to this run: the LLM key, the Pinecone key, the signer secret — all masked
a dispatch takes only ten inputs, so the non-secret settings arrive as one JSON blob
registry, storage account and vault names are derived from the slug, within Azure's limits
an Azure deploy still signs in to AWS, through OIDC, for this step and nothing else
GitHub OIDC token, subject tenant-{id}, exchanged by Entra ID for a short-lived token
storage account cbtf{slug}, container tfstate — Entra ID only, locked by a blob lease
registry, chatbot identity and its AcrPull grant, placeholder image URIs, then a 90 s wait
the registry had to exist first; this is the step the two applies exist to separate
vault and its secrets, storage, database, workspace, environment, apps — real image URIs now
Terraform creates the function app; its code is deployed separately, right here
succeeded or failed, carrying the chatbot URL and the signer URL
Resource group and container registry
created alone, ahead of everything else, because the next step needs somewhere to push
the container app is still described with a placeholder image at this point
Both images, inside the tenant's registry
chatbot-backend and chatbot-frontend, tagged with this deployment's version
only now can a container app be created that actually starts
Everything else, created by the second apply
Key Vault, and the secrets written into it in the same apply that creates it
Storage account and a private blob container for the knowledge base
Log Analytics workspace and the Container Apps environment bound to it
Container App: frontend and backend in one replica, sharing localhost
App secrets from Terraform variables; images pulled by identity
docs-signer Function App, its plan and its own runtime storage account
A custom role scoped to the storage account: delegate, write, delete. No read, no list.
PostgreSQL Flexible Server with the vector extension allow-listed — when chosen
A Pinecone index in the customer's own project — when that store was chosen instead
Each secret arrives as a Terraform variable, so its plaintext is present in the runner's
memory during this step. Masking keeps it out of the log, not out of the process.
The function app exists here but cannot serve yet: its code is pushed at step 10.
What the platform knows when the run ends
The chatbot URL and signer URL, plus the resource group, storage account, container and vault names Terraform assigned — the names it could not know before the run.
As on AWS it keeps no standing access, and reaches documents only through the signer URL using the shared secret it generated at onboarding.
Two differences from the AWS pipeline are structural rather than cosmetic. Terraform runs twice because a registry must exist before an image can be pushed into it, and a container
app cannot be created against an image that is not there. Every tenant secret passes through the runner, because the vault that will hold it is created by the very same run.
One incidental dependency is worth noting for the evaluation: an Azure deployment still authenticates to AWS twice, for the source images and for the Terraform state backend.
